title: Massage for Arthritis

content:
Massage can help some people with arthritis feel less stiff and more relaxed for a short time, but it does not treat the arthritis itself. NICE says manual therapy such as massage should only be used alongside exercise for osteoarthritis, not on its own. Gentle massage is usually safe, but avoid pressing on a joint that is hot, red and swollen.

How massage may help

Arthritis pain is not just about the joint. Muscles around a sore joint often tighten to guard it, and that tension adds its own ache. Massage may help by:

  • easing muscle tightness and spasm around the joint
  • warming tissues so movement feels easier afterwards
  • calming the nervous system and reducing stress, which affects how strongly we feel pain
  • improving sleep for some people

The effects are usually short-lived, from hours to a day or two. That makes massage most useful as a way to get moving: a gentle massage followed by your exercises can make the exercise more comfortable.

What UK guidance says

NICE's osteoarthritis guideline (NG226) says do not offer manual therapy, which includes massage and joint manipulation, unless it is alongside therapeutic exercise. In other words, massage can be a helpful add-on but should not replace strengthening and activity.

For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE (NG100) focuses on disease-modifying medicines and access to physiotherapy and occupational therapy. Massage is not part of standard RA treatment, but many people use it for comfort.

When to avoid or adapt massage

Do not massage directly over a joint that is:

  • hot, red and swollen. This may be an active flare or, more rarely, an infection that needs urgent assessment.
  • recently injured, broken or operated on, unless your surgeon or physiotherapist says it is fine

Take extra care, and tell the therapist, if you:

  • take blood thinners or bruise easily, including from long-term steroids
  • have osteoporosis. Firm pressure over the spine or ribs is not advised.
  • have numbness, poor circulation, varicose veins or a history of blood clots. A hot, swollen calf needs medical advice, not massage.
  • have fragile skin, psoriasis or lymphoedema
  • have fibromyalgia, where firm pressure may feel painful. Lighter pressure is often better.

Massage should not cause sharp pain. A good therapist will adjust the pressure and ask how you feel.

Self-massage you can do at home

You do not need to pay for massage to get some benefit. Try:

  • Hands: rub a little hand cream into each finger, stroking from the tip towards the palm. Gently circle your thumb across the palm.
  • Knees: sitting with your leg supported, stroke the thigh muscles above the knee with flat hands for a few minutes. Avoid pressing hard on the kneecap.
  • Neck and shoulders: use the opposite hand to knead the top of the shoulder gently, or lean against a wall with a soft ball between your back and the wall.
  • Feet: roll your foot slowly over a tennis ball or a cold drinks bottle while seated.

Warming the area first with a warm bath, shower or wheat bag often makes self-massage more comfortable. Keep it gentle and stop if pain increases.

Professional massage in the UK

Massage for arthritis is not usually available on the NHS. Physiotherapists may use soft tissue techniques as part of a wider treatment plan. Privately, look for a therapist with a recognised qualification and insurance, and ask whether they have experience with arthritis. Sports massage is often too firm for inflamed joints, so ask for a gentler approach if needed.

Making massage part of a bigger plan

Massage works best as one tool among several:

  • daily movement and strengthening exercises
  • pacing your activity across the day
  • heat for stiffness and cold for hot, swollen flares
  • the medicines your GP or rheumatology team recommends

If you find you need massage more and more just to keep going, that is a sign to review your treatment with your GP, physiotherapist or rheumatology team.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
